title: Rosemary-infused oil for muscle pain
subtitle: A warming oil for sore, aching muscles
excerpt: Dried rosemary infused into olive oil at low heat, then massaged into sore or aching muscles. Traditionally used in western herbal practice as a warming topical preparation. Makes about 200 ml, enough for many applications. Keeps 12 months in a dark glass bottle.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931) : rosemary entry, external uses for circulation and muscular complaints. EMA HMPC monograph on Salvia rosmarinus (2010) : traditional-use assessment for external preparations. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983) : rosemary preparations, topical application for muscular rheumatism.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prepare in batches and decant into small amber bottles. Keeps 12 months stored correctly.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in a cool, dark cupboard in amber glass. Discard if the oil smells rancid or develops a sour note.

glossaryTerms.definition: A carrier oil that has been gently heated or cold-infused with dried plant material to draw out fat-soluble constituents. Different from an essential oil, which is a steam-distilled concentrate.

content.text: Rosemary-infused oil is dried rosemary steeped in olive oil over low, steady heat, then strained and bottled for use as a massage oil. The ratio is one part dried rosemary to five parts olive oil by weight, held at 60 to 65 degrees Celsius for two to four hours. It comes out a pale gold with a strong, resinous rosemary scent. Rub it into sore or aching muscles after exercise or at the end of a long day. The oil keeps 12 months in a dark glass bottle stored away from heat and light.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms. This preparation is for external use only: it is rubbed into the skin, not taken by mouth. Rosemary at therapeutic dose carries a pregnancy caution; consult a herbalist or your midwife before using this oil in pregnancy. At the dilution used here the topical risk is low, but the caution applies as a general guideline. Rosemary has no significant drug interactions at this preparation strength.

items.prepNote: dried (not fresh : moisture causes mould in the oil)
light olive oil or extra-light; avoid strong-flavoured varieties

content.text: Step 1: Set up the double boiler

Fill a saucepan with about 5 cm of water and set a heatproof bowl on top so it sits above, not in, the water. Add the dried rosemary and olive oil to the bowl. The herb must be fully dry before it goes in; any moisture will make the oil go cloudy and eventually mouldy.

Bring the water to a gentle simmer. Clip a probe thermometer to the edge of the bowl and keep the oil between 60 and 65 degrees Celsius throughout. This is a gentle, steady warmth, not a fry. Too hot and you degrade the volatile components you want in the oil. Too cool and the infusion takes much longer. Stir occasionally. After two hours the oil should smell strongly of rosemary and take on a slightly deeper colour. Continue for up to four hours for a more concentrated result.

attrs.title: Temperature is the main failure mode
attrs.body: A probe thermometer is the most useful tool in this preparation. The oil should sit between 60 and 65 degrees Celsius. A pan that is boiling hard will push the bowl temperature above 80 degrees, which is too hot. Keep the water at a low simmer and check the oil temperature every thirty minutes.

content.text: Remove the bowl from the heat and leave it to cool for 20 to 30 minutes. Line a sieve with a double layer of muslin over a clean jug. Pour the warm oil through and press the spent herb firmly to extract the last of the oil. Discard the herb. Pour the strained oil through a small funnel into a clean amber glass bottle. Label with the date.
Pour a small amount of the

into the palm of your hand and warm it between both palms for a moment before applying. Massage into the affected muscles using firm, circular strokes. For sore legs or back, apply after a bath or shower when the skin is warm and the pores are open. Wash hands after use if you do not want the scent on everything you touch.

Apply 2 to 5 ml per application (roughly a teaspoon) to the affected area, up to three times a day. Massage in thoroughly. There is no strict course limit for this external preparation, but if soreness does not ease within five to seven days of regular use, see your doctor rather than continuing indefinitely.

Pour into clean amber glass bottles with tight-fitting lids. Store in a cool, dark cupboard away from heat and direct light. The oil keeps for 12 months. Check periodically: if it smells rancid, sharp, or sour it has gone off. Discard and make a fresh batch.
When not to use this remedy

Do not apply to broken skin, open wounds, or inflamed skin. Do not use in pregnancy without checking with your midwife or a herbalist first. See a doctor for sudden severe muscle pain, muscle pain with dark urine, muscle pain with weakness or numbness, or any pain unrelated to physical effort and lasting more than a couple of weeks.

attrs.heading: What went wrong
attrs.intro: Common problems and what caused them.

items.symptom: The oil went cloudy or mouldy
items.cause: Moisture in the herb. Even a slightly damp batch will introduce water into the oil.
items.fix: Always use properly dried herb. Spread the dried rosemary on a tray and leave in a warm, airy kitchen for a day before using if you are unsure. The whole batch should be discarded if mould appears.

items.symptom: The oil smells cooked or burnt
items.cause: Temperature was too high for too long.
items.fix: Keep the oil between 60 and 65 degrees Celsius and check with a thermometer. A burnt-smelling oil should be discarded.

items.symptom: The oil has very little rosemary scent
items.cause: Either the herb was stale, or the infusion time was too short, or the temperature was too low.
items.fix: Use freshly dried rosemary (within the past 12 months). Infuse for the full four hours at the correct temperature.
